summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is criminalised in Comoros, and the sources disagree on the applicable penalty. The Human Dignity Trust country profile gives up to three years' imprisonment. Outright International, updated 12 March 2026, cites Article 300 of the 2020 penal code as carrying six months to two years plus a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 Comorian francs (US$240 to 720). A Washington Blade report of 23 December 2024 cites Article 318 with a maximum of five years. Whichever provision applies, a visitor should treat any same-sex intimacy, including private consensual conduct between adults, as carrying a real risk of arrest and imprisonment.

Enforcement is documented rather than hypothetical. Outright International records the first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy in 2022, following a leaked video. In June 2024 two women were arrested after asking an imam to marry them. On 12 December 2024 a Comoros court sentenced the pair to five and six months for homosexuality and released them with time served, an outcome Reuters reported the following week. Outright International describes the case as the first conviction of its kind, and the Human Dignity Trust called the prosecution a human-rights violation.

The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report states that authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions for same-sex conduct during 2023 and did not actively enforce the law. Police reported that they did not incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons, and no such violence was reported that year. The same report lists widespread impunity among the country's major human-rights problems, so the absence of prosecutions in a single year does not amount to legal protection.

No non-discrimination law protects LGBTIQ people in Comoros, and change of legal gender marker is not available. The government has repeatedly refused United Nations recommendations to decriminalise same-sex conduct.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement record is episodic, not absent: a period of no recorded prosecutions in 2023 sits alongside a first imprisonment in 2022, arrests in June 2024 and a conviction in December 2024. Non-enforcement in any given year offers a visitor no assurance about the next.

No known LGBTIQ organisation operates in the country. Article 5 of Law 86-006/AF discourages registration of such bodies, which removes the usual local point of contact for a traveller seeking advice, accompaniment or assistance after an arrest.

Widespread impunity is identified as a major human-rights problem in the US State Department's 2023 reporting, and the same department's 2010 report on Comoros documents poor prison conditions alongside other civil-liberties restrictions. The 2020 penal code cited by Outright International differs from the provisions named in the Human Dignity Trust and Washington Blade accounts, so the operative instrument itself should be confirmed against primary text.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same criminal provision as visitors, with no anti-discrimination statute to fall back on and no legal mechanism for changing the gender marker on identity documents.

Police stated in 2023 that they neither incite nor tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons, and none was recorded that year, but no non-discrimination law backs that position and widespread impunity persists as a documented national problem.

Article 5 of Law 86-006/AF chills registration of LGBTIQ organisations, and none are known to exist, so resident LGBTIQ people have no registered advocacy or legal-aid body to approach.
outOfScopeNotes:
Which article of the penal code governs same-sex conduct, and what penalty it carries, is unresolved across the sources: three different articles and three different maximum penalties appear (three years, two years plus a fine, and five years).

Entry and visa requirements for transgender travellers, document screening at ports of arrival, and access to gender-affirming care are not addressed by any source reviewed here, so no finding is offered on those points.

The US State Department's 2010 report on Comoros contains limited LGBT content and was not relied on beyond noting that limitation; the substantive US findings here come from its 2023 report.
